paras: The killing of the Campbell brothers was the mob killing of Bud and Reilly Campbell, two men described as 'desperadoes', at their house in Caldwell County, Kentucky, in August 1882. A mob of 25 to 40 men besieged the house at night, set it on fire and killed both brothers, losing one of its own members in the gunfire. Wire reports carried the story nationally within a day, and in October it was retold at length as the prelude to the lynching of Mary Sullivan.

According to a Louisville Commercial feature published in October, the Campbells had lived in the Tradewater River bottoms of northern Caldwell County and were linked by neighbors to a series of smokehouse and store robberies. The brothers later rented a small grocery about four miles away on the public road to Princeton, where, a day or so before the attack, they fired on a party of drinking Princeton men after one of them discharged a pistol. The Hopkinsville South Kentuckian likewise reported that the two had been in a shooting scrape the day before, in which no one was killed.

The mob came at night; the South Kentuckian counted 25 men, while the Commercial described forty masked riders armed with shotguns. The Commercial said the leader first ordered the McMurtry family, an old man and small children living in the cabin, to leave before the firing began. About 150 shots were fired, according to the South Kentuckian, and the attackers lost one man, whom the Commercial named as Hice Johnson, a farmer who bled to death on the road.

The mob then set the house on fire. In the August wire version, the brothers were 'riddled with bullets' as they were driven out, while the South Kentuckian said they were captured and hurried away and Bud was later found dead a few yards off. The Commercial's account had Reilly shot dead inside the cabin and Bud, his ammunition gone, staggering out of the fire, where a dozen men bound him, dragged him into the woods and hanged him.

No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution for the killing of the Campbells was found. Soon afterward Crockett Jenkins, described as another member of the gang, was found hanged near Princeton, and Mary Sullivan, who had been tried and released for his death, was taken from a house and hanged by a mob on Sept. 29. The Madisonville Times said it was not known whether Sullivan's killers were the 'Regulators or Vigilants' who had hanged the Campbells or friends of the gang.

The first reports came from a Paducah or Cincinnati dispatch printed on Aug. 13 in papers from Knoxville and St. Paul to Cheyenne and Seattle, under headlines such as 'Death of Desperadoes' and 'Desperadoes' Fate.' Condensed versions ran in news summaries over the following weeks, some misplacing the house in 'Campbell County' and one stating that 'all of the boys' died. Kentucky papers added local detail but shared the wire's view of the victims, the South Kentuckian ending its report with the remark that they 'had long been a terror to the community.'

In October the killing resurfaced in coverage of Mary Sullivan's lynching, which the Martinsburg Independent headed 'Wholesale Lynching in Kentucky' and described as a gang 'being rapidly decimated by the outraged people.' The Louisville Commercial's long narrative, reprinted in Washington, St. Paul and South Carolina, gave the brothers' names and a dramatized account of the siege and hanging. None of these reports mentions the race of the brothers or of the mob.

The accounts disagree on the date: the August wire and summaries point to Saturday, Aug. 12, one roundup says Friday, the South Kentuckian gives a Tuesday night, and the October dispatches put the hanging about three weeks before early October. Because the wire was in print on Aug. 13, the attack cannot have occurred later than Aug. 12, and the October dating appears to be a retelling error.

bases: A mob of 25 to 40 men besieged two brothers described as desperadoes, killed one in or near the burning house, and, in the fuller accounts, captured the other and carried him away and killed him, hanging him in the woods according to the Louisville Commercial (A3, A14, A28, A31).

The August wire report, the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian, the Madisonville Times and the Louisville Commercial feature independently report that a mob killed the Campbell brothers of Caldwell County, though they differ on the date and on how each died (A3, A14, A22, A28).

accounts.label: Louisville dispatch and Madisonville Times
accounts.gist: Two Campbells and another member of the gang were taken out and hanged by a mob of citizens, attributed by the Madisonville Times to 'Regulators or Vigilants.'

accounts.label: Louisville Commercial feature
accounts.gist: Forty masked men besieged the grocery cabin after the Campbells fired on Princeton riders; Hice Johnson of the mob and Reilly Campbell were shot dead; the cabin was fired and Bud, coming out, was bound, dragged into the woods and hanged.

framing.detail: August papers across the country ran the short wire under headlines such as 'Death of Desperadoes' and 'Trapped and Killed', calling the brothers 'desperadoes' and giving no names.
The South Kentuckian closed by saying the brothers 'had long been a terror to the community', and the Martinsburg Independent described the gang as being 'rapidly decimated by the outraged people.'
The Louisville Commercial feature treated the killing as a dramatic episode in Mary Sullivan's story, describing the mob's 'hatred in their hearts' and calling the dying mob member 'respectable.'
